ui.hero.title: Benzodiazepines & the GABA<sub>A</sub> receptor
ui.hero.lead: Benzodiazepines (BZDs) are positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) of the GABAA receptor. They bind at the extracellular α+/γ2− interface, distinct from the two orthosteric GABA sites at the β+/α− interfaces, and increase the apparent affinity of GABA, thereby increasing the frequency of Cl− channel opening without gating the channel in the absence of agonist. This resource integrates receptor structure, subunit pharmacology, drug properties and pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic models.
ui.mechanism.title: Allosteric modulation at the receptor
ui.mechanism.intro: Cryo-EM structure of the human α1β3γ2 GABAA receptor in complex with GABA and diazepam (PDB 6HUP; Masiulis et al., Nature 2019), shown as a simulated density map in a lipid nanodisc. Choose the GABA concentration, a BZD-site ligand and its dose (or set the free concentration directly), the α isoform and, optionally, flumazenil; the readouts give the BZD-site occupancy, the apparent GABA EC50 and the open probability. The animated channel opens in bursts and desensitises according to a kinetic scheme of the receptor, and Cl− ions cross the 9′ gate while it is open. Below the viewer, the neuron type and membrane potential set the direction and size of the Cl− flux and the GABA reversal potential, and a plot shows how the receptors open and desensitise during a GABA application and recover after washout.

ui.subunits.title: Receptor subunits & clinical effects
ui.subunits.intro: The GABAA receptor family comprises 19 subunits (α1-6, β1-3, γ1-3, δ, ε, θ, π, ρ1-3); the predominant synaptic isoform is α1β2γ2 with a 2α:2β:1γ stoichiometry. High-affinity BZD binding requires a γ2 subunit and an α1, α2, α3 or α5 subunit bearing a conserved histidine (α1 His101, rat numbering). Point-mutation studies in mice attribute sedation and anterograde amnesia mainly to α1-, anxiolysis to α2/α3-, and aspects of learning and tolerance to α5-containing receptors. The cards below summarise the six α isoforms, with fractional BZD-site occupancy for the ligand and free concentration selected in Allosteric modulation at the receptor (kept in sync with Pharmacodynamics), and the β, γ2 and δ subunits; selecting an α card sets the isoform for all simulations.
ui.subunits.distributionIntro: Relative abundance of each α subunit by brain region on a brain model built from neuroimaging templates, shown as a rotatable 3D model or as a 2D map rendered from it; one hemisphere is translucent to expose the deep structures (thalamus, striatum, hippocampus, amygdala, hypothalamus), brainstem and cerebellum. Select an isoform to switch the map; the selection applies to all simulations. Hover over a structure for the cell populations concerned.

ui.routes.title: Administration routes & onset of action
ui.routes.intro: Seven routes of administration (IV, intranasal, buccal, rectal, sublingual, IM, oral) compared by onset, time to peak concentration and systemic bioavailability, with emphasis on the emergency treatment of seizures.
ui.pd.title: Pharmacodynamics
ui.pd.intro: Allosteric model with competitive binding at the BZD site: the fractional BZD-site occupancy is θ = (C/Ki) / (1 + C/Ki + Cflu/Kflu) and the apparent GABA EC50 is EC50app = EC50 / [1 + (β − 1)·θ], where C is the free ligand concentration and Ki its dissociation constant, Cflu and Kflu those of flumazenil, and β the cooperativity factor of the ligand (β > 1, PAM; β = 1, neutral antagonist; β < 1, inverse agonist/NAM). A pure PAM shifts the GABA concentration-response curve to the left without altering Emax.
ui.pk.title: Pharmacokinetics
ui.pk.intro: One-compartment model with first-order absorption and elimination, including active metabolites (e.g. nordiazepam, temazepam and oxazepam after diazepam) and patient- and interaction-related modifiers acting on specific elimination pathways (CYP3A4, CYP2C19, glucuronidation, renal excretion).
ui.pk.accumulationTip: Repeat the dose until steady state is reached
ui.pk.metabolismIntro: Most BZDs undergo hepatic phase I oxidation (CYP3A4, CYP2C19) before phase II glucuronidation, often yielding pharmacologically active metabolites with long half-lives; lorazepam, oxazepam and temazepam are glucuronidated directly. These pathways determine the modifier effects simulated above.
ui.dose.title: Dose-dependent effects & the ceiling effect
ui.dose.intro: Graded clinical effects with increasing dose and the plateau imposed by positive allosteric modulation, contrasted with sedative-hypnotics that gate the channel directly and with co-administered CNS depressants. Curves are computed for the ligand selected in Pharmacodynamics.
ui.dose.overdoseTitle: Benzodiazepine overdose and loss of the ceiling
ui.notes.title: Notes & limitations
ui.notes.parameterValues: Parameter values. Pharmacodynamic parameters (Ki, cooperativity factor β) and population pharmacokinetic parameters (t½, Vd, F, ka) are taken from FDA prescribing information, the IUPHAR/BPS Guide to Pharmacology, ChEMBL and primary papers, rounded for teaching; reference concentration ranges are indicative only. The source and verification status of each value are listed in the data tables.
ui.notes.pharmacodynamicModel: Pharmacodynamic model. A single allosteric term shifts the apparent GABA EC50 in proportion to BZD-site occupancy. Receptor reserve, desensitisation, state-dependent binding and differences between synaptic and extrasynaptic populations are not represented.
ui.notes.subtypeSelectivity: Subtype selectivity shows affinity only. The selectivity radar plots binding affinity (pKi) per α isoform, without separate potency (pEC50) or efficacy plots. In this model the allosteric shift scales linearly with occupancy and each ligand has one cooperativity factor β for all isoforms, so potency follows pKi within about 0.2 log units and efficacy is uniform; such plots would duplicate the affinity profile. For the clinical agents included, this matches their pharmacology: classical BZDs are non-selective in efficacy, and zolpidem's α1 preference is one of affinity. Efficacy selectivity - compounds such as L-838,417 or TPA023 that bind α1 without potentiating it - is real but outside the scope of this model.
ui.notes.pharmacokineticModel: Pharmacokinetic model. One compartment with first-order absorption and elimination. Distribution kinetics are therefore absent: the single-dose effect of lipophilic agents such as diazepam is in reality shortened by redistribution from brain to peripheral tissue, which this model does not capture. For the same reason the early peak of such drugs is underestimated (about 3-fold for oral diazepam). Absorption rate constants were fitted to the time to peak reported in FDA labels or primary studies, and the model was then compared with independent single-dose studies: predicted peak concentrations were within 2-fold of observed values in most cases (see the validation in the data tables). The onset of action and Tmax shown in the administration-route card are clinical values.
ui.notes.freeConcentration: Free concentration. Derived as peak plasma concentration × unbound fraction, assuming free brain concentration approximates free plasma concentration and ignoring active transport and protein-binding displacement. Occupancy uses the parent drug only: active metabolites (e.g. nordiazepam after diazepam) are not included, so occupancies at clinically equivalent doses are not directly comparable between drugs.
ui.notes.combinedExposure: Combined exposure. In the plasma profile, parent drug and active metabolites are summed as concentrations without adjustment for differing potency.
ui.notes.doseResponseCurves: Dose-response curves. Illustrative: GABA tone 5 µM at α1-containing receptors, with 1× dose set to ≈ 30% occupancy. Clinical effect bands and the opioid interaction term are approximate and chosen for teaching, not fitted to data.
ui.notes.regionalDistribution: Regional distribution. Abundance levels are a qualitative summary of immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridisation, mainly in rodent brain; human distribution is broadly similar but less completely mapped. Levels are relative within each isoform and not comparable in absolute receptor density between isoforms. Each structure is shaded uniformly, so laminar and nuclear differences (e.g. α3 confined to the reticular thalamic nucleus) appear only in the descriptions. The 3D brain combines the fsaverage cortical surface with structures segmented from the MNI152 2009c template, aligned by bounding boxes (accurate to a few millimetres); the hypothalamus, olfactory bulbs and spinal cord are approximated by simple shapes, and the cerebellar folia are rendered, not modelled. The 2D map is a lateral view rendered offline from the same model and coloured in the page, so it does not require WebGL; it is shown automatically if the 3D view is unavailable.
ui.notes.channelGating: Channel gating and Cl⁻ flux. The 3D view animates a single receptor with the kinetic (Markov) scheme of α1β3γ2L receptors of Haas and Macdonald (1999; rate constants as corrected in the 2004 erratum): two GABA binding steps, three open states with bursts of brief closures, and fast, intermediate and slow desensitised states. In the animation GABA is applied at the selected concentration in repeating cycles of application and washout (timing shown under the gate state), so activation, desensitisation, deactivation and recovery recur; the time course of a 4 s application and the recovery after washout are plotted below the viewer. Animation time is slowed 20-fold, and the gate is drawn open for each burst of openings (the brief closures within a burst are not drawn). A BZD-site ligand multiplies the GABA association rate at both binding steps by the EC50 shift of the allosteric model, so openings become more frequent while open and burst durations stay unchanged (Rogers et al., 1994; Lavoie and Twyman, 1996). Other studies place the BZD effect on a preactivation step after GABA binding (Gielen et al., 2012), and the slower deactivation of IPSCs seen in neurons (Mellor and Randall, 1997) is not reproduced by this mechanism. The scheme was measured with GABA alone, not with any BZD-site ligand: every ligand uses the same scheme and differs only through its occupancy and cooperativity factor, which set its EC50 shift; drug-specific kinetic effects are not modelled. The scheme was derived from recombinant receptors at 22-23 °C and is used for all α isoforms; the open probability readouts use this scheme, whereas the concentration-response and dose-effect curves use the equilibrium allosteric model, which has no desensitisation. The simulated IPSC in Pharmacodynamics has the rise and biexponential decay of IPSCs in cultured hippocampal neurons (Jones and Westbrook, 1995), with decay prolonged by PAMs as calibrated to Mellor and Randall (1997). Single-channel currents follow the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equations: the Cl⁻ permeability follows from γ = 27 pS in symmetrical 140 mM Cl⁻, and HCO₃⁻ permeates with PHCO3/PCl = 0.18 (HCO₃⁻ 25 mM outside, 15 mM inside). Extracellular Cl⁻ is 130 mM; intracellular Cl⁻ is 8 mM in a mature neuron (ECl = −74.5 mV, EGABA = −67.7 mV) or 30 mM in an immature neuron, where Cl⁻ uptake by NKCC1 before KCC2 expression keeps it high and GABA depolarises. Vm is adjustable (default −65 mV; 37 °C). In the mature gradient the Cl⁻ current rectifies outwardly (Bormann et al., 1987), so at the default Vm an open channel carries 0.047 pA of Cl⁻ current, far less than γ(Vm − ECl) predicts. The net Cl⁻ flux readout is Po × iCl/e at the peak and at steady state of the kinetic scheme. In the animation, ions reach the gate from the side the net flux comes from, at a rate proportional to it (none at ECl, where the unidirectional fluxes balance); they pass only while the gate is open and otherwise return, without queuing, so the mean flux is proportional to the open probability. Only net flux is drawn, and counts are scaled for display (scale shown under the flux readout). Membrane potential and ion concentrations are held constant: the voltage change caused by the current, Cl⁻ accumulation and saturation of permeation are not modelled. Flumazenil returns the flux to the GABA-alone level; it does not block the channel.
ui.notes.structure: Structure. The displayed structure is the α1β3γ2 template (PDB 6HUP); other α isoforms are indicated by colour and labels only, and sequence differences are not modelled. Ligands other than diazepam and flumazenil are shown on the diazepam pose.

ui.rx.info.beta:
β2/β3 subunit

Orthosteric sites: contributes the principal (+) face of the two GABA-binding sites at the β+/α− interfaces.

Transmembrane sites: β+/α− cavities in the TMD bind general anaesthetics (propofol, etomidate) and, at micromolar concentrations, diazepam (low-affinity sites).
ui.rx.info.gamma:
γ2 subunit

BZD site: provides the complementary (−) face of the high-affinity BZD site at the α+/γ2− interface; receptors lacking γ2 (e.g. αβδ) are BZD-insensitive.

Synaptic localisation: required for postsynaptic clustering of GABAA receptors via gephyrin.
ui.rx.info.bzdSite:
Benzodiazepine site (α+/γ2− interface)

Location: extracellular domain, formed by loops A-C of the α subunit (including α1 His101, rat numbering) and loops D-F of γ2.

Mechanism: BZD binding increases the apparent affinity of GABA (EC₅₀ typically 2-3-fold lower) and the frequency of channel opening, but does not gate the channel in the absence of GABA.

Antagonism: flumazenil binds competitively without intrinsic efficacy (β ≈ 1) and reverses BZD effects.
ui.rx.info.gabaSite:
Orthosteric GABA sites (β+/α− interfaces)

Stoichiometry: two sites per pentamer; occupancy of both is required for efficient channel gating.

Allosteric coupling: BZD binding at the α+/γ2− interface increases the apparent affinity of GABA at these sites.
ui.rx.info.pore:
Chloride-conducting pore (M2 helices)

Structure: lined by the five M2 helices; the 9′ leucine ring forms the activation gate and the −2′ region the anion-selectivity filter.

Gating: BZDs increase the frequency of channel opening, whereas barbiturates prolong the mean open duration and, at high concentrations, gate the channel directly.

ui.pk.accum.single: Accumulation. During repeated dosing, plasma concentrations rise until the rate of elimination equals the dosing rate; steady state is approached after 4-5 elimination half-lives. For {drug}, the longest-lived active species has t½ ≈ {t} h, corresponding to ≈ {time} to steady state. Select Show accumulation to simulate repeated dosing.
ui.pk.accum.item: t½ ≈ {t} h → R ≈ {r}×, 90% of steady state after ≈ {time}
ui.pk.accum.multi: Accumulation at a dosing interval of {tau} h. Because each dose is administered before the preceding dose has been eliminated, pre-dose (trough) concentrations (◆) rise until steady state. The accumulation ratio R = 1/(1 − e−kτ), where k is the elimination rate constant and τ the dosing interval, relates steady-state to first-dose exposure.
ui.pk.accum.clinical: Clinical relevance. The long-lived active metabolite {met} continues to accumulate after {drug} itself has reached steady state. Sedation, psychomotor impairment and the risk of falls may therefore increase over 1-2 weeks of treatment, particularly in older adults, in hepatic impairment or with CYP inhibitors, and may persist for several days after discontinuation. Agents without active metabolites that are cleared by direct glucuronidation (e.g. lorazepam, oxazepam) are therefore preferred in older patients.
ui.pk.note.imDiazepam: Intramuscular diazepam: owing to poor aqueous solubility, diazepam precipitates at the injection site and absorption is slow and erratic (Tmax ≈ 1-2 h); IV, rectal or intranasal/buccal routes are preferred in emergencies.
ui.pk.note.imGood: Intramuscular administration: rapid and reliable absorption (bioavailability > 90%) supports IM use in status epilepticus when IV access is unavailable and in acute agitation.
ui.pk.note.summary: Pharmacokinetic summary. Population elimination half-life of {drug}: ≈ {t} h.
ui.pk.note.met: Active metabolite. {name} (t½ ≈ {t} h) prolongs the duration of clinical effect beyond elimination of the parent drug.
ui.pk.cmp.summary: Duration of action. Plasma concentrations after a single oral dose, normalised to each drug's Cmax, so that only the time course is compared. Time from peak to 50% of Cmax: {list}{mods}. The decline reflects the elimination half-life: midazolam (high hepatic clearance) suits procedural sedation and sleep induction; oxazepam, alprazolam and lorazepam give short-to-intermediate durations, with oxazepam and lorazepam cleared by direct glucuronidation without active metabolites (hence their use in older adults and hepatic impairment); clonazepam (t½ 30-40 h) gives a long duration without clinically relevant active metabolites; and diazepam persists for days. In practice, the single-dose effect of lipophilic agents such as diazepam is shorter than their half-life suggests because of redistribution from the brain to peripheral tissues (not represented in this one-compartment model), whereas the long half-life and active metabolites dominate during repeated dosing.
ui.pd.cr.sumAntagonist: Neutral antagonism. {flu} occupies the BZD site (θ = {occ}%) without intrinsic efficacy (β ≈ 1); the apparent GABA EC₅₀ remains {ec} µM. It has no effect of its own but competitively displaces PAMs, which underlies its use in reversing BZD sedation.
ui.pd.cr.sumNam: Negative allosteric modulation. {drug} (β = {b}) decreases the apparent affinity of GABA (apparent EC₅₀ {ec} µM; rightward shift), an action associated with anxiogenic and proconvulsant effects.
ui.pd.cr.sumCompetitive: Competitive antagonism. {flu} (θ = {occ}%) displaces {drug} from the α+/γ2− site, returning the apparent GABA EC₅₀ toward baseline ({base} µM; current {cur} µM).
ui.pd.cr.sumPartial: Partial positive allosteric modulation. {drug} has limited efficacy at {sub} (β = {b}, versus ≈ 3 for full PAMs): apparent EC₅₀ {base} → {cur} µM ({fold}-fold). Partial efficacy was pursued to retain anxiolytic activity with less sedation, ataxia, tolerance and dependence.
ui.pd.cr.noModulation: {drug} does not modulate receptors containing this α isoform.
ui.pd.cr.sumPam: Positive allosteric modulation. The GABA EC₅₀ decreases from {base} to {cur} µM ({fold}-fold leftward shift) while Emax is unchanged, consistent with an increase in apparent agonist affinity rather than direct agonism.

ui.pd.occ.flu: {flu} competes for the same site and shifts all curves to the right.
ui.pd.ipsc.sum: Synaptic inhibition. By increasing GABA affinity at sub-saturating synaptic concentrations, BZDs prolong IPSC decay (weighted τdecay {base} → {tau} ms) and increase inhibitory charge transfer, with little change in peak amplitude when receptors are near saturation.

ui.pd.dose.noteAntagonist: {drug} occupies the site without intrinsic efficacy (β ≈ 1); the curve remains at the endogenous baseline, which explains its ability to reverse BZD effects without producing effects of its own.
ui.pd.dose.noteNam: {drug} reduces GABAergic inhibition below baseline (β < 1), producing anxiogenic and proconvulsant rather than sedative effects.
ui.pd.dose.notePartial: {drug} is a partial agonist (β ≈ {b}) with a lower ceiling (≈ {c}%), favouring anxiolysis over sedation.
ui.pd.dose.notePam: {drug} attains ≈ 90% of its maximal effect at ≈ {x}× the usual therapeutic dose; further dose escalation adds little effect.
ui.pd.dose.summary:
Dose-dependent effects. With increasing dose, BZDs produce a graded sequence of effects: anxiolysis, anticonvulsant and myorelaxant activity, sedation and ataxia, and hypnosis with anterograde amnesia. Anxiolysis occurs at low receptor occupancy and is mediated by α2/α3-containing receptors; anticonvulsant activity arises at low occupancy and involves α1- as well as α2/α3-containing receptors, whereas sedation and amnesia require higher occupancy of α1- (and α5-) containing receptors.

Ceiling effect. As positive allosteric modulators, BZDs enhance the action of endogenously released GABA but do not gate the channel in its absence. At saturating occupancy, the maximal effect is therefore bounded by synaptic GABA availability and by the cooperativity factor β (≈ 2-3 for full PAMs). Taken orally without other CNS depressants, BZDs therefore rarely cause fatal respiratory depression, in contrast to barbiturates, which directly activate the channel at high concentrations. This margin does not apply to rapid or high-dose intravenous administration: intravenous midazolam is used to induce anaesthesia and can cause apnoea, particularly in older or critically ill patients.
ui.pd.dose.model: Illustrative model: GABA tone {gaba} µM, {sub}-containing receptors, 1× dose ≈ {occ}% occupancy; opioid effect {op}% alone, amplified up to {amp}-fold with increasing BZD-site occupancy. Effect bands are approximate.
ui.pd.dose.warn:
Benzodiazepine alone. The ceiling depends on endogenous GABA: BZDs only amplify GABA-evoked chloride currents and cannot open the channel on their own, which gives them a wide therapeutic index. Most overdoses of a BZD alone cause drowsiness, ataxia, slurred speech and amnesia that resolve within 12-36 h. Deaths from a BZD alone are rare but do occur, mainly out of hospital, where an unconscious person's airway is not protected: in older adults, in chronic respiratory or cardiac disease (COPD, obstructive sleep apnoea), after very large doses, and with the more toxic agents (e.g. temazepam, flurazepam, alprazolam).

Loss of the ceiling with co-ingestants. Opioids, ethanol and other CNS depressants (gabapentinoids, barbiturates, sedating antidepressants, antipsychotics and antihistamines) depress the CNS through other mechanisms, so the combined effect exceeds the BZD ceiling and reaches the zone of respiratory depression (dashed red curve; the opioid is modelled at a usual therapeutic dose). Most fatal BZD overdoses involve such co-ingestants, particularly opioids, and the risk rises with the BZD dose.

How death occurs. (1) Central hypoventilation: opioids suppress the brainstem respiratory rhythm generator (pre-Bötzinger complex) and the ventilatory responses to CO2 and hypoxia; BZDs and ethanol add GABAA-mediated depression, giving a supra-additive fall in breathing. (2) Upper-airway obstruction: deep sedation relaxes the pharyngeal muscles, so the tongue and soft palate obstruct the airway, particularly in the supine position, while suppressed arousal prevents waking. (3) Hypercapnic-hypoxaemic respiratory failure then leads to bradycardia, cardiac arrest and hypoxic brain injury, often unwitnessed during sleep. (4) Complications of coma: aspiration of gastric contents, hypothermia and the consequences of prolonged immobility.

Management. Supportive care is the mainstay: airway protection, oxygenation and ventilation, recovery positioning and circulatory support; naloxone reverses the opioid component of a combined overdose. Flumazenil is reserved for selected patients, because it can precipitate seizures in BZD dependence or with pro-convulsant co-ingestants (e.g. tricyclic antidepressants), and its short action allows re-sedation.

ui.st.displacedText: {flu} ({occ}%) competitively displaces {drug}. As a neutral antagonist (β ≈ 1) it removes the EC₅₀ shift, so Cl⁻ influx returns to the GABA-alone level; GABA still opens the channel. Clinically, it reverses BZD sedation but may precipitate withdrawal seizures in dependence.
